# Third Pass — the supplement brief

*Same shape as before: the market hasn't been named. I'm going to stop waiting for that and choose one, on the reasoning below. If it's the wrong choice, the reasoning will be easier to argue with than a request for clarification would have been.*

**Japan.** Because it is the market where this category is currently in the most interesting trouble, and trouble is where the cheap advantage lives.

---

## What we are actually walking into

Japan does not need to be taught that supplements exist. Penetration is high, the shelf is crowded, and the regulatory architecture — the notification-based *functional claims* route, where a company files its own evidence rather than having it approved — was built on the assumption that firms would behave.

Then, in 2024, a red-yeast-rice product was linked to serious kidney injury and a number of deaths, and it emerged that the interval between the manufacturer knowing and the public knowing was measured in months. The category did not lose awareness. It lost the benefit of the doubt.

So the brief is not "how do we get noticed." Every competitor is solving for noticed. The brief is: **what would a company do differently if it assumed the buyer had already decided we were probably lying?**

Most of what follows is that question answered literally.

## Claim less than the law permits — and put the gap on the pack

We are legally entitled to file a functional claim. I would file a narrower one than our evidence supports, and then state, on the label, in plain Japanese, what we *deliberately chose not to say*.

Something to the effect of: *the trial showed an effect at this dose, over this period, in this population. It did not test anything else. We have not claimed anything else.*

This reads as absurd to a marketing department and as extraordinary to a Japanese consumer, because under-claiming is a recognised social register here — it signals confidence rather than weakness. Boasting is the tell of someone with nothing. A restrained claim is not a smaller claim; in this market it is a *more credible* one, and credibility is the entire scarce resource right now.

The effect size, incidentally, should be published as a number rather than an adjective. If it's modest, say modest. The people who will not buy on a modest number were never going to repurchase anyway.

## Publish the recall trigger before we need it

The single most valuable asset available to us costs nothing and would be resisted by everyone: state publicly, at launch, what would cause us to withdraw the product, and commit to a disclosure clock — any credible adverse-event report published within seventy-two hours, whether or not causation is established, whether or not it turns out to be ours.

The last scandal was not fundamentally about a contaminant. It was about a delay. We can pre-commit against the delay, in public, and let the commitment be the campaign. Note that this only works if it is genuinely binding, which means legal and PR must be told about it rather than consulted about it. If we run this past an approvals chain it will emerge as a wellness pledge and be worthless.

Adjacent, and cheap: batch-level assay results, the actual contract manufacturer named, a QR on every unit that resolves to *that* lot rather than to a brand page. Opacity in the supply chain was the whole failure. We can simply not have one.

## Mibyō, not transformation

Japanese health culture is organised less around cure than around 未病 — the state before illness, the drift that hasn't become a diagnosis yet. The corresponding ethic is maintenance, continuation, not falling out of balance. Not optimisation. Certainly not the Western before-and-after arc, which is legally constrained here anyway and, more importantly, culturally reads as a promise made by someone who won't be around to keep it.

So the creative territory is *continuity*: the ordinary week, protected. Nobody is transformed. Somebody simply keeps doing what they were already doing. Quiet, seasonal, unpeopled by celebrities.

## Buy the calendar, not the airtime

Two timings matter more than any media plan.

The weeks after the annual health check results arrive. Tens of millions of people receive a set of numbers about themselves, in a fairly narrow window, and experience a brief, genuine, self-directed intent to do something. That is not a fear appeal — the anxiety exists without us, and arrives by post. We are simply present, factual, and non-catastrophising at the moment it lands.

And the seasonal health vocabulary that already exists: 夏バテ, the summer collapse; 花粉 season; the rainy weeks; winter 冷え. These are shared, spoken, un-invented. A brand that speaks the market's existing health calendar back to it doesn't have to manufacture an occasion.

## The person who is actually asked

The decisive conversation is not our advertisement. It is thirty seconds in a drugstore aisle with a staff member who has been asked *is this all right with my mother's blood pressure medication.*

I would put the budget there. Train them, honestly, including on interactions and on who should not take this — the elderly on multiple prescriptions, the pregnant, the people for whom the answer is see a doctor first. Give them a card that says who this is wrong for, and make it as prominent as the one saying who it's right for.

There is a KPI hiding in this that I would like us to actually adopt: **count the sales we decline.** Publish it internally. A month in which we talked nobody out of buying is a month in which the training didn't take.

## Stealth is now illegal, so let's overshoot the law

Undisclosed advertorial has been an unfair representation here since late 2023. Everyone will comply to the line. I'd sit visibly beyond it — label gifted product, label seeded product, label the relationship even where no money moved, and instruct anyone we work with that they are free to publish a negative verdict without consequence. Written down, given to them, in advance.

Ninety percent of the value of that instruction is that it exists and can be shown to people. The remaining ten percent is that occasionally someone uses it, which is the proof.

## The subscription is where the goodwill dies

Auto-renewing, hard-to-exit supplement subscriptions are among the most complained-about consumer practices in this market and have already drawn legislative attention. They also, for a period, work beautifully on the spreadsheet.

I would refuse them entirely. No minimum term, no count contracts, cancellation in one tap without a retention call, and a proactive email at month three asking whether the customer still wants it. Some proportion will say no. That number is the price of the trust, and it is smaller than the number who quietly resent us into permanent non-repurchase — a cohort I've mentioned before, in another context, and which nobody ever measures because it doesn't file complaints.

## What I'd resist

The white coat. The 「No.1」 badge and its footnote. The tarento endorsement, which in this category now transfers risk to the celebrity rather than credibility to us. Any headline containing the word *breakthrough*. The LINE funnel that begins helpful and becomes a drip. And an English-language creative concept translated locally, which is always identifiable and always costs more to repair than it saved.

## Measurement

Not recall, not reach. Repurchase at 180 days. Unprompted recommendation rate among drugstore staff who receive nothing for it. Declined sales. And the ratio of adverse-event reports we surfaced ourselves to those surfaced by others — a metric that looks like a liability and is in fact the entire strategy in one number.

---

The through-line, said once and then not repeated: we are not competing on efficacy, because in a post-scandal category nobody believes efficacy claims and the ones who do are not the ones who stay. We are competing on **verifiability** — and verifiability is largely free, structurally awkward, and almost never chosen, which is precisely why it's available.

Which leaves two questions rather than the one I've been carrying. The first is still open. The second is whether we would honour the seventy-two hour clock on a Friday afternoon in a quarter that was already going badly.

I'd want that answered before the creative work starts, not after.
